source.title: Sample-Size Scaling of the African Languages NLI Evaluation
source.authors: Anuj Tiwari; Oluwapelumi Ogunremu; Terry Oko-odion; Jesujuwon Egbewale; H. Nwokocha

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses prior scaling-law work but its experiments vary evaluation-set sample size, not model parameters, training tokens, training compute, or pretraining loss. It explicitly distinguishes evaluation reliability from learning curves.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates fixed models on randomly subsampled AfriXNLI test examples; model parameters are not adjusted. Its sample-size results concern the reliability and behavior of evaluation accuracy, not the training-data scaling or held-out pretraining loss in the claim. The authors explicitly state that they are testing evaluation, not learning.
record.test_reason: The study varies only evaluation-set subsample size (50–500 test examples) for two fixed ~0.6B models. It does not change parameters, training tokens, compute or pretraining loss, so no version is tested. Kaplan, Hoffmann and Muennighoff appear only in related work.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that small evaluation subsets give high-variance, optimistically biased accuracy estimates, and that trends are language-specific and non-monotonic. They recommend at least 300 evaluation samples and stress that this is evaluation reliability, not learning. Note that the abstract frames the work as labelled-data scaling, but the experiments only subsample test sets.
record.recipe_differences: No reproduction or test of the original scaling-law methods; the experiment changes test-set subsample size while holding model parameters fixed.
record.method_sensitivity: Evaluation trends and saturation points vary by language; the paper also reports different absolute accuracy and variance levels between the two models.

fits_no_version.finding: Accuracy estimates from small random test subsets are high-variance and often higher than estimates from larger subsets. The authors put stabilisation at roughly 200–450+ examples, varying by language. All accuracies are near 3-class chance (about 24–41%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benchmark accuracy estimates on small test subsets are unstable and can be optimistically biased, independent of model scaling.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 7th Workshop on African Natural Language Processing (AfricaNLP 2026)
record.problems: The experiments use only AfriXNLI and two models, both roughly 0.6 billion parameters. They measure evaluation behavior rather than learning dynamics. Numerical details for the main plotted aggregate and language-specific trends are not stated in the text descriptions; the number of random subsampling runs is not stated.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix Tables 2–33 give separate accuracy, precision, and F1 results by language, model, and sample size. They are not extracted as individual rows because they report evaluation-subset performance, not any tested version of the claim; the selected rows capture the paper's explicit qualitative findings relevant to that distinction.

untested.parts: No variation of parameters, tokens or compute; no pretraining loss.
No other modality or training regime scaled. Fine-tuning data size is not varied; only test-set size is.
Downstream accuracy is not related to model scale or pretraining loss.

record.verdict_notes: Every reported accuracy is close to or below 3-class chance. This suggests the models barely perform the task, which undermines even the paper's own interpretation. The study is irrelevant to every scaling-law version.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not vary model parameters, training tokens, or compute and does not measure held-out pretraining loss or power-law fits.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger training runs is tested.
No compute budget, training allocation, or loss-minimising parameter/token split is tested.
The study does not compare architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime is tested; the experiment concerns evaluation-set subsampling for African-language NLI.
The study does not measure downstream performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss; it measures accuracy on differently sized evaluation subsets.
The study does not estimate scaling-law exponents or test how fitting choices affect them or compute-optimal allocations.

rows.subject: all languages and models (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Two models, each roughly 0.6 billion parameters
rows.operation_detail: Compared accuracy-estimate variability across randomly subsampled evaluation-set sizes.
rows.measure: Standard deviation of accuracy across subsampling runs; the paper reports a rapid decrease as sample size increases and stabilization after an average of 300 samples.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation across runs is the measure; numerical values are not stated in the figure description.
rows.note: This is evaluation-estimate variance, not training loss or a learning curve.

rows.subject: XLM-R Large
rows.operation_detail: Compared accuracy-estimate variability across randomly subsampled evaluation-set sizes.
rows.measure: Standard deviation of accuracy; high variance at smaller evaluation sizes and stabilization with larger sets.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation across runs is the measure; numerical values are not stated in the figure description.
rows.note: The reported result concerns evaluation-set variability.

rows.subject: AfroXLM-R Large
rows.operation_detail: Compared accuracy-estimate variability across randomly subsampled evaluation-set sizes.
rows.measure: Standard deviation of accuracy; high variance at smaller evaluation sizes and stabilization with larger sets.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation across runs is the measure; numerical values are not stated in the figure description.
rows.note: The reported result concerns evaluation-set variability.
rows.check: The stage is unclear: the paper does not say how AfroXLM-R Large was given an NLI head. Its accuracies sit near 33% chance throughout.

rows.subject: XLM-R Large
rows.operation_detail: Measured NLI accuracy on increasingly large randomly subsampled evaluation sets.
rows.measure: Accuracy declines as evaluation sample size increases; the text describes the decline as monotonic.
rows.note: The authors interpret this as small-sample evaluation optimism and changing instance representativeness, not a change in model learning.
rows.check: Value is not figure-only. Appendix Table 6 gives XLM-R Yoruba accuracy 35.33% at n=50 and 28.87% at n=500. This is evaluation-subset size, not model scale.

rows.subject: XLM-R Large
rows.operation_detail: Measured NLI accuracy on increasingly large randomly subsampled evaluation sets.
rows.measure: Accuracy rises slightly up to around 150 examples, then decreases and stabilizes.
rows.note: The outcome is a non-monotonic evaluation-subset trend, not a training learning curve.
rows.check: Value is readable from Table 7: 30.00% at n=50, 34.22% at n=150, 32.28% at n=500. Not a scaling-law measure.

rows.subject: AfroXLM-R Large
rows.operation_detail: Measured NLI accuracy on increasingly large randomly subsampled evaluation sets.
rows.measure: Accuracy decreases as evaluation sample size increases; the text says the qualitative trend is similar to that for XLM-R Large.
rows.note: The authors interpret the pattern as evaluation bias, not a change in model learning.
rows.check: Value is readable from Table 23: AfroXLM-R Yoruba 36.00% at n=50 and 33.27% at n=500. Not a scaling-law measure.

rows.subject: AfroXLM-R Large
rows.operation_detail: Measured NLI accuracy on increasingly large randomly subsampled evaluation sets.
rows.measure: Accuracy initially gains and then stabilizes; the text says the qualitative trend is similar to that for XLM-R Large.
rows.note: The outcome concerns evaluation-subset size, not training data scaling.
rows.check: Table 24 gives 34.67% at n=50, 36.00% at n=100, then about 32.3% at n=500. That is a decline after n=100, not simply 'gains then stabilizes'. Not a scaling-law measure.
